doc.title: Tom Varner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 13, 2025

title: Breakthrough in phrasing, Oberlin and switching to New England Conservatory
summary: He first tongued every note, then around 19 broke through to bebop phrasing; Oberlin was conservative, NEC welcoming, with Gunther Schuller and George Schuller.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Is that – I won’t even say easier – more possible to pull off by articulating each note more than slurring.

Yes. This is a very good point. In the beginning I sounded very stiff and corny because the only way I could get the notes to come out just right was to tongue every note. So it would be like [scats] I would sound like a ‘20s band. [scats] even if I’m trying to play bebop. And oh I remember how there was this breakthrough somewhere in the end of freshman or sophomore year, around 19ish, 18ish or 19ish I realized wait a minute. If I can get that phrasing better and not have to tongue every note I will have made a big leap of getting closer to the way we would want it to sound. And I forget whether it was summer of ‘—maybe summer of ’76, summer of ’77 – 18, 19 I was able to then finally be able to articulate phrases in a more of a bebop language way that a trumpet might do, or a tenor sax might do, and not have to tongue every note. And that was a big deal. I remember. Then it kind of felt like I was off and running. So I was at Oberlin for two years but I was not in their conservatory and there were so many good things, I made many good friends, some I’m friends with to this day. And bless him, you might have known Wendell Logan. L-O-G-A-N. He was one of the main teachers at Oberlin then. But he was like the one voice in the wilderness kind of. And they were very conservative back then. So I realized I needed a place that was going to be more supportive so I switched over to New England Conservatory. So I had two years at Oberlin, two years at New England Conservatory, and they were very different. They were like, “You want to play jazz on the French horn?” And at first they were like, “What?” And I was like, “Yes!” They were like, “Okay, come on in. Gunther will love this.” My first year there it was Gunther’s first year not there. Because I think he just wanted to do his own thing. He was tired of being a president. But I was always in touch with him and then I was in touch with maybe you’ve interviewed or for other projects George Schuller, his son, who is a great drummer and is also a kind of a keeper of the flame of the information of the Lenox jazz school and things that Gunther was up to and a lot of – and “Birth of the Cool” and a lot of those things. So I found a wonderful community then for those next two years.
